concepts.name: Basel Convention: Origin, Mandate and Legal Architecture
key_dimensions: Adopted in 1989, entered into force 1992 — distinguish these two dates as UPSC often tests entry-into-force vs. adoption
Negotiated under UNEP auspices — contrast with Rotterdam (FAO+UNEP) and Stockholm (UNEP only)
Core mandate: control transboundary movements of hazardous wastes AND their disposal — 'AND disposal' is frequently missed
Secretariat located in Geneva — contrast with Stockholm (Geneva) and Rotterdam (Geneva/Rome dual) for trap questions

concepts.name: Definition of 'Hazardous Waste' under Basel Convention
key_dimensions: Two-tier definition: Annex I categories PLUS Annex III hazardous characteristics (e.g., explosive, flammable, toxic) — both criteria must be met
Annex II wastes: household wastes and residues from incineration — separately listed, not covered by Annex I
Domestic law can expand the definition — parties may designate additional wastes as hazardous under national legislation
UPSC trap: electronic waste (e-waste) is NOT explicitly named in original text; its coverage via 'Basel Ban Amendment' and COP decisions is a grey area

concepts.name: Prior Informed Consent (PIC) Mechanism
key_dimensions: Exporting state must notify competent authority of importing AND transit states before movement — 'transit state' consent is frequently overlooked
Written consent of importing state is mandatory before shipment begins — oral or implicit consent is insufficient
Competent authority system: each party must designate a national competent authority — distinct from PIC under Rotterdam Convention (which covers chemicals, not wastes)
Failure to obtain PIC renders the movement 'illegal traffic' — legal consequences under Article 9

concepts.name: Basel Ban Amendment (Amendment to Article 4A)
key_dimensions: Adopted at COP-3 (1995): prohibits export of hazardous wastes from Annex VII countries (OECD + EU + Liechtenstein) to non-Annex VII countries — even for recycling
Entered into force September 2019 after crossing the 3/4th ratification threshold — decades-long delay is an important fact
India's position: India is a non-Annex VII country and a significant importer of recyclable hazardous materials — strategic implication
UPSC trap: The Ban Amendment covers waste FOR RECYCLING — parties often argue recycling is beneficial, making this the most contested provision

concepts.name: Illegal Traffic in Hazardous Waste: Definition and State Obligations
key_dimensions: Article 9 defines illegal traffic — includes movement without PIC, movement based on falsified documents, and movement not conforming to documents
Re-import obligation: if exporting state is responsible, it MUST take the waste back — 'duty to reimport' is a specific legal obligation
Criminal liability requirement: parties must enact domestic legislation to make illegal traffic a criminal offence
Distinction from 'accidental' transboundary movement — illegal traffic requires intent or negligence; accidental spillage has separate provisions

concepts.name: Environmentally Sound Management (ESM): Core Principle
key_dimensions: ESM is the overarching obligation — defined as taking all practicable steps to ensure wastes are managed in a manner that protects human health and environment
ESM is NOT a ban — it permits movement if ESM can be guaranteed at destination; this is the key distinction from the Ban Amendment
Basel Convention Technical Guidelines: non-binding guidance documents that operationalize ESM for specific waste streams (e.g., ship recycling, e-waste)
UPSC overlap trap: ESM under Basel vs. 'best available techniques' under Stockholm POPs Convention — different standards for different conventions

concepts.name: Waste Minimization and Proximity Principle
key_dimensions: Article 4(2)(a)-(b): parties must reduce waste generation and ensure disposal as close to source as possible — 'proximity principle'
Hierarchy: prevention > minimization > recovery/recycling > disposal — Basel follows this waste hierarchy
Obligation to prohibit export if importing country lacks capacity for ESM — exporter bears responsibility for assessing importer's capacity
Contrast with free-trade arguments: Basel explicitly overrides WTO free-trade principles for hazardous waste movements — tested in Shrimp-Turtle type questions

concepts.name: Basel Protocol on Liability and Compensation
key_dimensions: Adopted 1999, NOT YET IN FORCE — requires 20 ratifications; this 'not in force' status is a classic UPSC trap
Covers liability for damage during transboundary movement AND disposal of hazardous waste
Strict liability for the notifier/exporter during transit; fault-based liability after waste reaches disposal facility
Financial security requirement: operators must maintain insurance or bond — modeled on similar provisions in nuclear liability conventions

concepts.name: Basel Convention and E-Waste: Specific Provisions and COP Decisions
key_dimensions: E-waste not explicitly defined in 1989 text — classified under existing Annex categories (e.g., lead, mercury-containing wastes)
Basel COP-9 (2008) and COP-10 (2011): adopted specific technical guidelines for ESM of e-waste — distinguishes 'used equipment' (not waste) from 'e-waste'
The 'used vs. waste' loophole: exporters label non-functional electronics as 'second-hand goods' to bypass Basel — a well-known evasion technique
India's E-Waste Management Rules 2016/2022: domestic implementation — Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) is the key mechanism; compare with Basel obligations

concepts.name: Ship Recycling and the Hong Kong Convention: Overlap with Basel
key_dimensions: Ships at end-of-life contain asbestos, PCBs, heavy metals — qualify as hazardous waste under Basel
Hong Kong International Convention for Safe and Environmentally Sound Recycling of Ships (2009, not yet in force) is the lex specialis for ship recycling
Contested overlap: Is a ship being sent for recycling a 'waste'? Basel parties argued YES; shipping industry argued NO — COP decisions affirm Basel's applicability
India relevance: Alang (Gujarat) is world's largest ship-breaking yard — subject to Basel scrutiny; Supreme Court directions in Research Foundation case

concepts.name: The Basel, Rotterdam and Stockholm (BRS) Conventions: Synergies and Distinctions
key_dimensions: Three separate legal instruments but share a joint secretariat since 2010 — administrative synergy ≠ legal merger
Basel: hazardous WASTE movements; Rotterdam: prior informed consent for hazardous CHEMICALS and pesticides in trade; Stockholm: elimination/restriction of POPs
A substance can be simultaneously covered: e.g., PCBs are regulated under Stockholm (elimination) AND their waste under Basel — overlapping obligations
UPSC trap: 'Which convention deals with persistent organic pollutants?' — Stockholm, NOT Basel; Basel deals with their waste disposal aspect only

concepts.name: Annex Structure of Basel Convention: Annexes I–IX
key_dimensions: Annexes I & II: waste categories; Annex III: hazardous characteristics; Annex IV: disposal operations (D-list) and recovery operations (R-list)
Annex VIII (List A): wastes presumed hazardous — require full Basel controls; Annex IX (List B): wastes NOT covered unless contaminated — UPSC often tests this reversal
Recovery operations (R-list) vs. Disposal operations (D-list): R1–R13 vs. D1–D15 — key for determining if movement is for 'recycling' or 'final disposal'
Amendment to Annexes: requires COP decision + ratification by parties to enter into force — annexes are NOT automatically amended

concepts.name: India and the Basel Convention: Ratification and Domestic Implementation
key_dimensions: India ratified Basel Convention in 1992 — among early ratifying developing countries
Hazardous and Other Wastes (Management and Transboundary Movement) Rules, 2016 (amended 2019): primary domestic legislation implementing Basel
India has NOT ratified the Basel Ban Amendment (as of knowledge cutoff) — strategic position as a recycling economy
Supreme Court: Research Foundation for Science v. Union of India — directed government to implement Basel obligations for ship-breaking; landmark case

concepts.name: Conference of Parties (COP) to Basel Convention: Decision-Making
key_dimensions: COP meets every two years — odd-numbered years; decisions by consensus, failing which by 2/3 majority of parties present and voting
COP-15 (2022, Geneva): first joint COP of BRS conventions — 'COPs MOP' terminology for conventions with both COP and Meeting of Parties
Plastic waste amendments adopted at COP-14 (2019): added plastic waste to Annex II and created Annex IX (B3011) exemption for clean, uncontaminated plastic scrap
UPSC trap: COP decisions are binding on parties but annexe amendments require separate ratification — distinguish binding decisions from recommendatory guidelines

concepts.name: Plastic Waste Amendment to Basel Convention (2019)
key_dimensions: Entered into force January 1, 2021 — relatively recent, high UPSC relevance
Requires PIC for export of 'contaminated, mixed or non-recyclable' plastic waste from developed to developing countries — clean, sorted plastic remains in Annex IX (less regulated)
Context: China's 2018 'National Sword' policy banning plastic waste imports triggered this amendment
India's stance: India amended its Hazardous Waste Rules to align; Plastic Waste Management Rules 2016 (amended 2022) are the domestic counterpart

concepts.name: Financial Mechanism and Technical Assistance under Basel Convention
key_dimensions: No dedicated financial mechanism like GEF for Basel — contrast with Stockholm and Minamata which have GEF as financial mechanism
Basel Convention Regional Centres (BCRCs): 14 regional centres globally for capacity building and technology transfer — India hosts BCRC for South and Southeast Asia in Mumbai
Technical assistance is a 'best efforts' obligation on developed countries — not a legally binding financial commitment
UPSC trap: 'Which environmental convention uses GEF as its financial mechanism?' — Stockholm YES, Basel NO; Basel relies on voluntary contributions

concepts.name: Distinction Between 'Hazardous Waste' and 'Other Wastes' under Basel
key_dimensions: 'Other wastes' (Annex II) includes household waste and incineration residues — subject to Basel controls but NOT classified as hazardous
Practical implication: 'other wastes' still require PIC for transboundary movement — the PIC obligation is broader than just hazardous wastes
Radioactive wastes are EXCLUDED from Basel — governed by IAEA conventions; this exclusion is a frequent UPSC trap
Wastes arising from ships' normal operations are excluded — covered under MARPOL Convention; another classic overlap trap

concepts.name: Relationship Between Basel Convention and WTO Agreements
key_dimensions: Basel restrictions on waste trade can conflict with GATT Article XI (prohibition on import/export restrictions) and Article XX (general exceptions)
MEA–WTO conflict resolution: WTO dispute panels have not definitively ruled on Basel-WTO hierarchy — theoretical tension remains
Basel Article 11 allows bilateral/multilateral agreements on hazardous waste — provided they are 'no less environmentally sound' than Basel; WTO-compatible route
UPSC angle: 'Can a country ban hazardous waste imports under WTO law?' — Yes, under GATT Article XX(b) (human/animal/plant life) — Basel provides the legitimate objective

concepts.name: National Competent Authorities and Focal Points: Institutional Obligations
key_dimensions: Each party must designate at least one competent authority and one focal point — dual institutional requirement
Competent authority: responsible for receiving notifications, granting/refusing consent — operational role
Focal point: responsible for transmitting and receiving information to/from the Secretariat — informational/diplomatic role
India's competent authority: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC) through CPCB for technical matters — tested in context of bilateral waste shipments

concepts.name: Compliance Mechanism and Enforcement under Basel Convention
key_dimensions: Compliance Committee established by COP-6 (2002): non-confrontational, non-judicial, assistance-oriented — contrast with adversarial WTO dispute settlement
No punitive sanctions mechanism — relies on peer pressure, technical assistance, and reputational consequences
Reporting obligations: parties must submit annual reports on transboundary movements — low compliance rate among parties is a known weakness

UPSC trap: 'Does Basel Convention have a binding dispute settlement mechanism?' — Article 20 provides for ICJ referral or arbitration but is rarely invoked; Compliance Committee is the primary mechanism
